title: CMS Extends 2026 Home Health Moratorium

sections.text: What the CMS Home Health Moratorium Means for You

sections.content: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has extended its temporary freeze on new Medicare enrollment for home health agencies in certain high-risk areas through 2026. This freeze, known as a moratorium, stops new agencies from enrolling in Medicare in a handful of designated counties and states where fraud risk and provider oversaturation have been a long-standing concern.

This is not a reduction in your Medicare benefits. The moratorium targets new business enrollment, not the home health services you are entitled to under Original Medicare or a Medicare Advantage plan.

sections.calloutText: If you already receive care from a home health agency enrolled in Medicare, that agency can continue treating you and accepting new patients. The moratorium only blocks newly forming agencies from entering the affected markets.
sections.calloutTitle: Your current care is not at risk

sections.text: Why CMS Keeps Extending This Moratorium

sections.content: CMS first introduced home health moratoriums to address a pattern it saw in a few metro areas: a sudden surge in new agencies enrolling in Medicare, far beyond what the local population of eligible patients could justify. That kind of rapid, unexplained growth has historically been associated with improper billing and, in some cases, outright fraud schemes that drained Medicare trust fund dollars without delivering real care.

The moratorium has been renewed periodically because CMS continues to see elevated fraud risk indicators in specific regions, even as it works through other enforcement tools. You may have seen broader Medicare program integrity efforts covered in the news, including data-driven audits and provider screening changes. This moratorium is one piece of that larger effort, described in CMS program integrity materials, to keep Medicare spending tied to legitimate, medically necessary care.

CMS publishes and periodically updates the specific states and metro areas under moratorium status, and those designations have historically concentrated in a small number of markets rather than applying nationwide.

sections.text: Which Regions and Services Are Affected

sections.content: The moratorium applies narrowly. It affects new Medicare enrollment of home health agencies in specific counties within designated states, not hospice care, not home-based primary care visits from your doctor, and not every type of home-based service nationwide.

items: States and metro areas historically included: parts of Florida (notably the Miami metro area), Illinois (Chicago area), Michigan (Detroit area), and Texas (Houston and Dallas areas) have been subject to home health moratoriums in past CMS designations.
Agency types affected: the freeze applies to newly enrolling home health agencies, meaning businesses that have not yet completed Medicare enrollment in the designated counties.

Services excluded from the freeze: hospice agencies, physician home visits, durable medical equipment suppliers, and home health agencies that were already enrolled before the moratorium took effect are not subject to the new-enrollment freeze.

sections.content: Existing, already-enrolled home health agencies in these regions are not frozen out of the market. They can continue accepting new patients. The moratorium simply prevents additional competitors from entering, which keeps the existing pool of agencies serving patients without interruption.

sections.text: Does This Affect Hospice Care Too

sections.content: Hospice care falls under separate CMS rules. CMS has at times issued distinct hospice enrollment moratoriums in different regions, but these are tracked and announced independently from home health moratoriums. If you or a family member rely on hospice services, the home health moratorium described here does not apply to that care.

To check whether your specific hospice provider is affected by any separate hospice-related enrollment action, you can ask the hospice agency directly whether it is currently enrolled and in good standing with Medicare, or confirm its status using the Medicare.gov care compare tool.

sections.text: How This Could Affect Your Access to Care

sections.content: The reasonable concern here is access. If no new agencies can enter a moratorium region, an area that already has limited home health options could see longer wait times or fewer choices, particularly in neighborhoods where demand for home health services is high relative to the number of enrolled agencies.

For most beneficiaries, this will not create a noticeable change. If you already have an established relationship with a home health agency, that agency remains enrolled, remains able to treat you, and remains able to take on new patients as its capacity allows.

If you are searching for a new home health agency in a moratorium region for the first time, perhaps after a hospital discharge or a new diagnosis, it helps to start that search early rather than waiting until the day you need care. Ask your discharge planner, primary care doctor, or hospital social worker which Medicare-enrolled agencies are currently accepting patients in your area, since they often track real-time availability more closely than online directories.

If you live in one of the regions under a home health moratorium, do not wait for a health crisis to find out which agencies are still accepting new patients. Call two or three Medicare-enrolled agencies in your area now, ask about current wait times, and keep that information on hand so you are not scrambling to compare options during an urgent situation.

sections.text: Steps to Take if You Need Home Health Services Now

sections.content: If you or a family member needs home health care right now, a few concrete steps can help you move forward without delay.

items: Ask your doctor for a referral to an already-enrolled agency. Your doctor's office often has an up-to-date list of agencies currently serving your area and accepting new patients.

Confirm Medicare certification status directly with the agency. Ask the agency to state clearly that it is Medicare-certified and currently in good standing, since certification status can change over time.

Verify coverage under Original Medicare or your Medicare Advantage plan. Under Original Medicare, any Medicare-certified home health agency can treat you. Under a Medicare Advantage plan, you may need to confirm the agency is in your plan's network, since many Advantage plans use provider networks that differ from Original Medicare's open access rules.
Contact your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) if you cannot find a provider. SHIP counselors offer free, unbiased guidance and can help you locate enrolled agencies in your area.

sections.content: The coverage verification step is where Original Medicare and Medicare Advantage differ most. Original Medicare pays any Medicare-certified home health agency the same way, regardless of which one you choose. A Medicare Advantage plan may require you to use an in-network agency to get full coverage, so a quick call to your plan's member services line before you start care can prevent an unexpected bill.

sections.text: How to Get Personalized Help Without Feeling Pressured

sections.content: It is normal to want more information before making any decision about your care or coverage, and you do not need to have every question answered on your own. A licensed Medicare agent can review your specific plan, walk through your home health coverage questions, and explain how the moratorium does or does not apply to your situation, at no cost to you.

Speaking with a licensed agent does not commit you to switching plans or making any change. Many people use this kind of conversation simply to get a second opinion on their current coverage, confirm their home health benefits are intact, and leave with a clearer picture before they need to act.

faqs.question: Do I need to switch my Medicare plan because of this moratorium?
faqs.answer: No. The moratorium does not require any plan changes. It only blocks new home health agencies from enrolling in specific high-risk counties. A plan review can still be worthwhile if you want to confirm your current home health benefits or you are unsure whether your preferred agency is in-network under a Medicare Advantage plan.

faqs.question: How do I know if my home health agency is still enrolled in Medicare?
faqs.answer: You can check an agency's Medicare enrollment status using the Medicare.gov care compare tool, or you can ask the agency directly to confirm it is currently Medicare-certified and in good standing. Both methods are free and do not require you to share personal health information.

faqs.question: Can I trust information about this moratorium that I find online?
faqs.answer: CMS.gov is the most reliable source for current moratorium regions and effective dates, since CMS updates its own program integrity pages directly. Be cautious of older articles that list outdated states or expiration dates, and consider confirming any claim against CMS's published materials or a licensed Medicare agent before acting on it.

faqs.question: What if I am worried about losing access to care later?
faqs.answer: A no-pressure plan review now can ease that concern by confirming your current home health benefits and identifying enrolled agencies in your area before you actually need care. This kind of check does not commit you to any changes; it simply gives you a clearer picture of your options ahead of time.

sections.text: Your Next Step for Peace of Mind

sections.content: The CMS home health moratorium is a fraud-prevention tool aimed at specific high-risk markets, not a cut to your current Medicare benefits. If you already have an enrolled home health agency, your care continues as before.

Taking a few minutes now to confirm your home health provider's enrollment status and review your plan's coverage details can prevent confusion later, especially if you live in one of the affected regions. If you want a clear, no-obligation look at how your coverage works, a [licensed Medicare agent](/medicare-supplement-plans/plan-g/) can walk through your specific situation and answer your questions directly.

seoDescription: CMS Medicare moratorium home health rules extended through 2026. Learn what this freeze means for your care and benefits.
excerpt: CMS extended its home health enrollment moratorium through 2026 in select high-risk areas, but your access to home health services under Medicare remains unaffected.
keyTakeaways: The moratorium freezes new home health agency enrollment in specific high-risk counties, not your Medicare benefits
Existing Medicare-enrolled home health agencies can continue treating current patients and accepting new ones
The policy targets fraud and provider oversaturation in a small number of metro areas, not nationwide
Hospice care and physician home visits are not covered by this home health moratorium
CMS periodically updates the specific states and counties affected by the moratorium
